en.title: VisionQuest Reveals Tommy Maximoff's Wild Comic Origins Just Got Weirder
en.summary: Marvel's VisionQuest is diving deep into the bizarre resurrection of Tommy Maximoff. The Disney+ series is already pushing boundaries, but the comics offer an even wilder look at Speed's twisted past.
en.body:
Fans were left reeling after **WandaVision** and are now getting a deeper dive into the Maximoff twins' fate with the **VisionQuest** series. The show has confirmed that Tommy Maximoff, presumed lost after Wanda's hex collapsed, is alive and well — sort of. Now known as Thomas Shepherd and played by **Ruaridh Mollica**, this Scottish speedster's survival is explained through a process eerily similar to Billy Maximoff's resurrection in **Agatha All Along**: a spirit finding a new host after a near-death experience. The series doesn't shy away from this inherent weirdness, embracing the complexity of Vision and Scarlet Witch's magically-infused, synthezoid offspring.

The journey of Tommy and Billy in the comics, however, takes the concept of 'weird' to a whole new level. Vision himself is a creation born from layered identities: the body of the original Human Torch fused with the 'brainwaves' of the deceased Wonder Man. This already makes him one of Marvel's most unique characters. His twin sons, Tommy and Billy, are products of Wanda's immense power and desire for a family, a magical construct that ultimately unraveled. The comics, unburdened by the visual constraints of television, explore even more outlandish scenarios for these characters.

## The Terror of the Baby Hands

To understand just how strange Tommy's comic book past truly is, one only needs to look at the cover of **Avengers West Coast #52** from 1989. The issue features the supervillain **Master Pandemonium**, a character whose very name is a testament to comic book absurdity. Dressed in flowing red sleeves and a horned mask, Pandemonium’s most striking feature isn't his villainous attire, but what he holds in place of his hands: two young boys. These aren't just any boys; they are depicted as monstrous, green-skinned children, a horrifying visual that hints at the darker, more surreal storylines the comics have historically explored. These boys are, in fact, Tommy and Billy, presented in a form that reflects their fractured existence as lost souls wandering between dimensions.

## What This Means for Fans

For fans invested in the intricate tapestry of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the exploration of Tommy's origins in **VisionQuest** is a significant event. It bridges the gap between the more grounded, albeit fantastical, MCU narrative and the utterly wild, often unhinged, storytelling of the comics. The decision to lean into the inherent strangeness of these characters, particularly their unique birth and survival methods, signals a commitment to honoring the source material's legacy. This approach not only satisfies long-time comic readers but also offers a compelling hook for newer audiences drawn to the MCU's expanding multiverse and its increasingly complex character arcs.

## What's Next

**VisionQuest** is slated to premiere in 2026 as part of Marvel Studios' ambitious slate of upcoming Disney+ series, joining the ranks of **Ironheart**, **Wonder Man**, and **Spider-Noir**. Fans will be eager to see how the series further unpacks the bizarre journey of Thomas Shepherd and his connection to the Maximoff legacy.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for VisionQuest season 1 episodes 1-2 . Speed has arrived! Years after Tommy Maximoff and his twin brother Billy seemed to disappear after their mother Wanda dropped her hex in WandaVision , VisionQuest reveals that Tommy somehow lives, now as a Scottish man called Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica). The second episode of VisionQuest shows us how this happened, as the drowning of young Thomas allowed for Tommy Shepherd’s spirit to find a new host, not unlike the way Billy Maximoff’s spirit found a home in the body of the late Billy Kaplan (Joe Locke) in Agatha All Along . That’s really weird. And, to its credit, VisionQuest doesn’t shy away from the weirdness. But TV can only go so far, even Marvel TV with a Disney budget. Comics are so much weirder, which means that the story of Speed outpaces VisionQuest when it comes to bizarre decisions. The Terror of the Baby Hands Anyone who needs evidence of comics’ appetite for weirdness need look no further than the cover to 1989’s Avengers West Coast #52, written and drawn by John Byrne. There, you’ll see supervillain Master Pandemonium standing triumphant over the California-based team of Earth’s Mightiest Heroes, including Vision and the Scarlet Witch. Master Pandemonium has a ridiculous name and he’s dressed in a ridiculous outfit, complete with flowing red sleeves and a horned mask that lets his curly black hair peak out from the top. But such things are to be expected among supervillains. The unusual thing about Master Pandemonium are his arms, specifically what he has in the place of his hands: two young boys, turned green and monstrous. Even more absurd are the variations of that same scene inside the issue, where Master Pandemonium has two normal young boys at the end of his arms. Those boys are Tommy and Billy, the twin sons of Vision and Wanda, and everything about them is weird. Vision is, of course, a synthezoid, an artificial human being made from the body of the Golden Age Human Torch and implanted with the “brainwaves” of Simon Williams a.k.a. Wonder Man, long dead by the time of Vision’s first appearance in 1969’s Avengers #57. Make no mistake: Vision is a wonder, a complex android capable of thought, self-awareness, and even emotional depth, as demonstrated by his love for Wanda. But Vision cannot reproduce, so when Wanda gave birth to a pair of twins in 1986’s The Vision and the Scarlet Witch #12, questions were raised. And those questions went mostly unanswered. Chalk it up to the power of love, chalk it up to a miracle, chalk it up to Wanda being a witch. Somehow, a synthezoid got her pregnant—with twins, no less! The Devil’s Due Eventually, an explanation for the miracle did come, in the story leading up to Avengers West Coast #52.
